title: Love is patient (1 Corinthians 13)
hookLine: written to a quarrelling church, not a wedding: love is patient, kind, not puffed up
last: NO LONGER A SERVANT, BUT A BROTHER.

cards: A wedding. Someone's cousin walks up to the microphone and reads: love is patient, love is kind. Everyone smiles at the couple.
But that's not where it was first read. It was first read out loud to a church in Corinth, a busy port city in Greece, and that church was a mess.
They'd split into fan clubs: I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Peter. Members were taking each other to court. At their shared meals, the wealthy ate first and the poor went hungry.
And they competed over whose spiritual gifts were the most impressive. In the middle of a long letter to them, Paul stops arguing and writes this.

teach.b: It starts with a warning to the show-offs, in the King James Bible: "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."
Impressive, and just noise. Then the well-known part: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up." Charity, from the Latin caritas.
The Greek word underneath is today's word: agape. It isn't the usual word for romance, or for friendship.

teach.h: AGAPE: LOVE THAT WILLS YOUR GOOD.
teach.b: Christian teachers describe it as the love that wills the good of the other, even when they're difficult. Christians say it's the love God has for the world. Now hear who it was for.

Suffers long: to a church where people kept suing each other. Envies not: to people jealous of each other's gifts. Not puffed up: earlier in the same letter Paul had told them, knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

teach.h: A MIRROR TO A QUARRELING ROOM.
teach.b: Line after line is a mirror held up to a quarreling room, a correction written with great tenderness. Love never fails, Paul goes on; everything else we have is partial: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."
And he ends: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."
Churches still read it at weddings, and it belongs there too. But it was written for the hardest kind of love: loving people you're in the middle of a fight with. Which is also what a marriage needs.

how: 1 Corinthians 13 is often read at Christian weddings and funerals, and churches also read it in Sunday worship. Some Christians learn its description of love by heart.

games.q: you're Paul. the church in Corinth is split, suing each other, and competing over gifts. in the middle of your letter, what do you write?
o: a list of who's right and who's wrong.
a portrait of love, held up like a mirror.
a threat to stop writing to them.
games.why: he writes charity suffereth long, and is kind, every line a quiet correction of what the church was doing.

practice: Bring to mind someone who tries your patience, and hold one of Paul's lines up against yourself, not them: suffers long, is kind, is not puffed up. Which is hardest with this person?
Picture one small way to be patient next time; if you pray, pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Agape. The Greek word for love that wills the good of the other; charity in the King James. The last word of our stretch through Acts and Paul's letters.

orig.note: Greek: love that wills the good of the other. In 1 Corinthians 13 the KJV renders it charity.

carryVoice: Your line: the greatest of these. Tomorrow, the saints begin: what a saint is. That's day eighty-nine.
